description.narrative:
Samarbetspartnern UNDP kommer att genomföra projektet Governance Reform Fund (GRF) - fas III. Denna insats är ett efterfrågestyrt stöd och är ett instrument för att snabbt och effektivt kunna tillmötesgå förfrågningar från Georgiens regering.
Syftet med GRF är att stödja utvecklingen av ett effektivt system för offentlig förvaltning med större möjligheter för regeringen att införa en nationell utvecklingsplan som stärker rättsstatsstatens principer och förbättrar förutsättningarna för demokratisk ansvarsutkrävande.
Följande mekanismer kommer att säkerställa att målet uppfylls: 1) Konsulttjänster på begäran (on demand)– kortsiktig riktad policyrådgivning och 2) Fond för kapacitetsutveckling– initiativ i form av projekt som successivt ska leda fram till reformer inom berörda institutioner. Syftet med projektet är att tillgodose nationella partners långsiktiga utvecklingsmål.
Det förväntas att minst femton projekt kommer att ges stöd under projektets livscykel. Av dessa bör minst tio projekt kunna bedömas som lyckade och ha lett till hållbara resultat.
Det förväntas att regeringens förmåga att genomföra reformer inom den offentliga sektorn kommer att stärkas genom detta stöd.

The cooperation partner UNDP will implement the project Governance Reform Fund (GRF) – phase III. This intervention is demand driven and will be used as an instrument for responding rapidly and effectively to the requests of the Government of Georgia.
The goal of the GRF is support to development of an efficient public administration system with a stronger capacity of the government to implement a national development agenda that will strengthen the rule of law and improve conditions for democratic accountability.
The following mechanisms will insure achievement of the goal: 1) On-Demand Consultancy services - targeted short-term policy advice and 2) Capacity Development Fund - sub-projects initiatives increasingly leading to the transformational change in the institutions. The project aims to better accommodate longer-term development objectives of national partners.
It is expected that at least fifteen sub-projects will be supported during the project lifetime and at least ten projects will be evaluated as successful and would have sustainable results.
It is expected that the capacity of the Government to implement public sector reforms will be strengthened through contribution to transformational change of supported institutions.

The goal of the Governance Reform Fund (GRF) project is to support the development of an efficient public administration system with a stronger capacity of the government to implement a national development agenda that will strengthen the rule of law and improve conditions for democratic accountability. The achievement of the above goal will be ensured through (1) Capacity Development Fund (CDF) - sub-project initiatives increasingly leading to transformational change in the institutions; and (2) On-demand [Consultancy] Services (ODS) - targeted short-term policy advice.
• Capacity Development Fund (CDF): CDF initiatives would address critical and immediate capacity development needs of public sector agencies. The project will continue to place more emphasis on the initiatives with mid- to longer-term implications. This implies preparing a conceptual background for the launch of longer-term initiatives in line with national needs and priorities that would a shift from short-term activity based operation to longer-term planning with a strategic vision in the supported agencies.
• On-Demand [Consultancy] Services (ODS): Such initiatives imply on-demand provision of a combination of national and international advisory services and technical expertise to the public agencies to develop their capacity for policy implementation and advancement of reform agenda.
The intervention´s outcome is defined as: by 2021 the Government has stronger capacities to formulate, implement and monitor policies in a participatory and evidence-based manner for improved service delivery with equal access to all.

sector.narrative: Public sector policy and administrative management

description.narrative:
This contribution has been specific as it is completely demand driven and therefore it was impossible to plan beforehand which state authorities would apply for sub-projects and what would be their specific requests. Because of this overall objective was defined as: "by 2021 the Government has stronger capacities to formulate, implement and monitor policies in a participatory and evidence-based manner for improved service delivery with equal access to all," as it was quoted in the relevant place of the intervention appraisal.
Having in mind this overall objective one may needs to look at Georgia's global rankings. The rankings show mixed picture of Georgia's performance.
Economically, Georgia enjoyed steady growth from 2015 until 2019, however the outbreak and spread of COVID-19 has had a significantly negative impact on the country, with rates of both poverty and unemployment increasing. Poverty was estimated to have risen by 5.4 percentage points in 2020, while unemployment rose sharply to 20.4% in the fourth quarter of 2020. Indeed, the Georgian economy fell into recession in 2020, with Georgias gross domestic product (GDP) declining by 12.3% year-on-year. Meanwhile, in the Ease of Doing Business Index, Georgia ranked 6th out of 190 countries in 2019, with its score increasing from 82.04 in 2018 to 83.28. Furthermore, Georgia has consistently been listed in the Open Budget Indexs top five countries worldwide, reaching an historic high in the regulatory quality and efficiency indicator in 2017. With an overall score of 77.2, Georgia has slightly improved its ranking under economic freedom, albeit staying in the same position (12th). Despite its improved score, Georgias score under trade freedom dipped from 88.6 in 2020 to 86.0 in 2021. Nevertheless, driven by rising global food and oil prices and the earlier depreciation of the Georgian Lari, the inflation rate spiked at 12.8% in 2021, marking a ten-year high.
Georgia has also made significant progress over the past three decades towards gender equality and womens empowerment (GEWE). However, available data and multiple assessments show that much work still needs to be done. Georgias ranking in the World Economic Forums Global Gender Gap Index (WEF GGGI) has also fluctuated in recent years. In 2021, Georgia was ranked 49th (out of 156 countries), compared to 90th in 2016. However, despite some positive changes, major challenges still exist regarding the political participation of women, womens economic empowerment, and access to healthcare.
Based on the World Banks (WB) 2015-2020 indicators, Georgias score in the governance indicator voice and accountability over the 2015-2020 period dropped from 57.64 to 50. Furthermore, in the WJPs Rule of Law Indexs civil justice indicator, Georgia now ranks significantly lower compared to its standing on other WJP indicators, as it sits 67th globally.
Georgias standing in some key democratic indices has been declining. In Freedom Houses Nations in Transit, Georgia fell in from 3.25 in 2020, to 3.07 in 2021, keeping the country in the transitional or hybrid regime category. According to that report, the key drivers of decline were problems identified in the election process, problems regarding the independence of the judiciary, cases of limiting media freedom, and right-wing attacks on non-governmental groups.
Because of this mixed picture of global indexes on Georgia's performance in democratic transition the project overall objective achievement assessed as satisfactory and not assessed as very satisfactory even though a majority of sub-projects implemented by GRF achieved specific results as they were planned.
